title: Reflection at Curved Surface
notes:
14.1 INTRODUCTION — Light shows many phenomena such as reflection, refraction, and diffraction.

To observe reflection of light, a reflecting surface is needed, which may be of any shape — flat or curved.

The curved surface may be concave or convex.

A special type of flat and curved surface made from glass is called a plane mirror and a curved mirror respectively.

14.2 REFLECTING SURFACE — A reflecting surface is a surface that reflects a beam of light.

There are two types of reflecting surfaces: (1) Smooth reflecting surface — Example: plane mirror.

(2) Rough reflecting surface — Examples: wall, cloth, surface of soap, floor.

A mirror is the best smooth reflecting surface.

RAY OF LIGHT — It is a straight-line path along which light travels.

It is represented by a straight line with an arrow: →(ray of light).

A single ray of light is not possible/practically realizable on its own; light always travels as a bundle of rays.

BEAM OF LIGHT — It is a collection of rays of light, or a bundle of light rays, which is emitted by a source of light.

There are 3 types of beam of light: (a) Parallel beam — all the rays of light are parallel to each other.

Figure: several arrows drawn parallel to one another pointing in the same direction (⇉⇉⇉⇉).

(b) Converging/Convergent beam of light — a collection of light rays where all light rays are converged to a single point.

Figure: several rays drawn from different directions meeting at a single point 'O' (rays shown converging into O).

(c) Divergent beam of light — light rays diverged from a single point.

Figure: several rays drawn spreading outward from a single point.

REFLECTION OF LIGHT (Definition) — Incident ray of light: A light ray striking/falling at a reflecting surface, or the light ray emitted toward a surface.

Reflected ray of light: The ray of light obtained/bounced off from a reflecting surface.

Normal: It is a perpendicular drawn to the surface at the point of incidence.

Figure: Diagram showing normal line 'N' drawn perpendicular to a horizontal reflecting surface at the point of incidence; incident ray 'I ray' approaches from upper-left making angle 'i' with the normal; reflected ray 'R ray' leaves toward upper-right making angle 'r' with the normal; the point where incident ray meets the surface is labeled 'point of incidence', with dotted line shown as the produced/extended incident ray beyond the surface.

Reflection of light is defined as: 'It is a phenomenon of light in which light rays bounce off a reflecting surface such that they return into the same medium by changing its direction.'

TYPES OF REFLECTION OF LIGHT — There are two types: (a) Regular reflection of light, and (b) Irregular reflection of light.

Figure: Two small diagrams at top of page — left diagram shows an incident ray and reflected ray meeting a normal line drawn on a rough/hatched horizontal surface; right diagram shows a single vertical normal line on another hatched horizontal surface (illustrating surface roughness at microscopic level).

REGULAR REFLECTION OF LIGHT — It is such a reflection of light in which the reflected beam of light remains parallel to that of the incident beam.

It takes place at smooth reflecting surfaces such as a mirror.

Figure: Several parallel incident rays striking a smooth horizontal surface (marked with hatching) and reflecting as parallel rays at equal angles, drawn converging toward and diverging from the same points on the surface, labeled 'Regular reflection of light'.

IRREGULAR (DIFFUSED) REFLECTION OF LIGHT — It is such a reflection of light in which the reflected beam of light gets diffused.

It is also called diffused reflection of light.

It takes place at rough reflecting surfaces.

Figure: Several parallel incident rays striking a rough/wavy horizontal surface and reflecting off in many different scattered directions, labeled 'Diffused reflection of light'.

OPTICAL IMAGE — It is a representation of a physical object formed by an optical system or an optical device.

There are two types of optical image: (a) Real image, and (b) Virtual image.

REAL IMAGE — It is an optical image which can be obtained on a screen.

It forms when two or more actual reflected or refracted rays of light meet at a point.

In case of a mirror, real image is formed in front of the mirror; in case of a lens, real image is formed on the opposite side of the lens.

Real image is always inverted.

VIRTUAL IMAGE — It is an optical image which cannot be obtained on a screen.

It forms at the point of intersection of two or more produced (backward-extended) reflected or refracted rays of light.

Figure: Diagram showing several rays diverging from a point on the left, striking a vertical mirror line, reflecting outward to the right; the reflected rays are extended backward (dashed/produced) behind the mirror line to meet at a single point on the right labeled 'Image formed' — illustrating that the virtual image is formed where the produced rays appear to meet, not where actual rays meet.

In case of a mirror, virtual image forms behind it.

In case of a lens, virtual image forms in front of it, i.e., on the same side as the object.

REAL OBJECT vs VIRTUAL OBJECT — An object that emits light is called a real object; it may be luminous (e.g., sun, glowing bulb) or non-luminous (e.g., book, table).

A point where converging rays appear to meet is called a virtual object — for example, the image of a real object in a plane mirror is a virtual image but acts as a virtual object for our eye.

For a real object O, the virtual image is I: in the absence of the mirror the rays would converge to point O, but due to the mirror's presence the rays reach point I instead.

Figure 14.6(a): Real Object — rays diverging from a point O above a mirror surface, reflecting off the mirror, with the reflected rays extended backward (dotted) to meet below the mirror at point I labeled 'Virtual Image'.

Figure 14.6(b): Real Image — rays converging toward a point I below a mirror surface (shown as dotted lines to a virtual object O), reflecting off the mirror surface and actually meeting above it at a point labeled 'Real Image', with O labeled 'Virtual Object' below the mirror.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN REAL AND VIRTUAL IMAGES — Real Image: (1) Can be obtained on a screen, e.g., image formed in our eye.

(2) Formed by actual intersection of reflected or refracted rays.

(3) It is inverted.

Virtual Image: (1) Cannot be obtained on a screen, e.g., image of a real object formed in a plane mirror.

(2) Formed by producing (extending backward) reflected or refracted rays.

(3) It is erect.

14.5 MIRROR — A smooth reflector of light whose one side is silvered is called a mirror.

A commonly used mirror (looking glass) is made by depositing a thin layer of silver metal on one side of a plane glass sheet; the silver layer is then protected by a coating of red lead oxide (PbO) paint.

In all kinds of mirrors, the silver layer acts as the reflecting surface.

Figure: Classification tree — 'Mirror' branches into 'Plane' and 'Curved'; 'Curved' branches into 'Spherical' and 'Cylindrical Mirror'; 'Spherical' branches into 'Concave' and 'Convex'.

LAWS OF REFLECTION OF LIGHT (detailed) — (1) The angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence, i.e., r = i.

(2) The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie at the same point of incidence, in the same plane.

Figure: Diagram of a concave mirror — object AB (an arrow, A at base on principal axis, B at top) placed in front of a concave mirror; two/three incident rays drawn from point B striking the concave mirror surface at different points, each reflecting according to i = r, and converging to form an inverted real image A'B' below the principal axis, labeled 'Inverted nature' and 'Real image'.

A second figure below shows a plane mirror: rays diverging from a point above, striking a flat horizontal mirror line, and reflecting outward; the reflected rays are extended backward (dashed) to meet at a point below the mirror labeled 'Virtual image'.

SUMMARY FIGURE — Virtual Image (detailed diagram): It is an optical image which cannot be obtained on a screen.

It forms at the point of intersection of two or more produced reflected or refracted rays of light.

Figure: A point source on the left emits several diverging rays; these rays strike a vertical mirror surface and reflect outward to the right; each reflected ray is extended backward through the mirror line (shown with arrows crossing behind the mirror) to converge at a single point on the right, labeled 'Image formed'.

Notes accompanying the figure: In case of a mirror, the virtual image forms behind it.

In case of a lens, the virtual image forms in front of it, i.e., on the same side as the object.

This is contrasted with Real object vs Virtual object as a labeled comparison at the bottom of the page.

14.4 OPTICAL IMAGE (textbook) — A representation of a physical object formed by an optical system is called an optical image, or simply image.

It is formed when reflected rays or refracted rays meet or appear to meet.

There are two types of image: (i) Real image — An image which can be obtained on a screen is called a real image.

It is formed when the light rays after reflection or refraction actually intersect.

The real image is inverted with respect to the object.

Example: an image formed in our eyes.

(ii) Virtual image — An image which cannot be obtained on a screen is called a virtual image.

It is formed when the light rays after reflection (or refraction) do not actually intersect but intersect when produced backward.

The light rays seem coming from an image.

The virtual image is erect or upright with respect to the object.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN REAL AND VIRTUAL IMAGES (table) — Real Image: (1) The image that can be obtained on a screen is called real image, e.g., the image formed in our eye is real image.

(2) It is formed by the actual intersecting of reflected or refracted rays.

(3) It is inverted.

Virtual Image: (1) The image that can't be obtained on a screen is called virtual image, e.g., the image formed in plane mirror is virtual.

(2) It is formed by producing in backward direction of reflected or refracted rays.

(3) It is erect.

Figure 14.6(a): Virtual Image for real object — Real Object O in front of a vertical mirror line; several rays from O strike the mirror and reflect outward; the reflected rays are extended backward (dotted) behind the mirror to converge at point I, labeled 'Virtual Image'.

Figure 14.6(b): Real Image for virtual object — Virtual Object O behind a vertical mirror line (shown with dotted converging lines toward O); rays converging toward O are intercepted by the mirror and actually reflected to meet in front at point I, labeled 'Real Image'.

REAL AND VIRTUAL OBJECT (textbook) — An object that emits light is called a real object.

The real object may be either luminous (e.g., sun, glowing bulb etc.) or non-luminous (e.g., book, table etc.).

A point where the converging rays appear to meet is called a virtual object.

For example, image of a real object in a plane mirror is virtual image but it is virtual object for our eye.

For real object O, the virtual image is I as in Fig.

14.6(a).

In absence of the mirror, the rays converge to point O, but due to the presence of the mirror the rays reach the point I rather than O.

So, O is the virtual object whose real image I is formed as in Fig.

14.6(b).

14.5 MIRROR (textbook) — A smooth reflector of light whose one side is silvered is called a mirror.

Commonly used mirror (looking glass) is made by depositing a thin layer of silver metal on one side of a plane glass sheet.

The silver metal layer is then protected by a coating of red lead oxide (PbO) paint.

In all kinds of mirrors, silver layer acts as the reflecting surface.

Figure: Classification tree — 'Mirror' branches into 'Plane' and 'Curved'; 'Curved' branches into 'Spherical' and 'Cylindrical Mirror'; 'Spherical' branches further into 'Concave' and 'Convex'.

REFLECTION OF LIGHT AT A PLANE SURFACE (textbook, intro) — Let us see how light is reflected from a plane surface (i.e., plane mirror) and then an image is formed.

Properties of image of a real object formed by a plane mirror: (i) It is virtual.

(ii) It is of the same size as the object.

(iii) It is erect.

(iv) Object distance and image distance are equal.

(v) It is laterally inverted.

Point object and extended object: An object having no physical extent is called a point object.

An object having length, width and height as shown in figure 14.7(a) and an object having length, width and height as shown in figure 14.7(b) is called an extended object.

Figure 14.7(a): Image for point object — Real Object O in front of a mirror; several rays from O strike the mirror; reflected rays extended backward converge at virtual image point I.

Figure 14.7(b): Image for extended object — Extended object AB in front of a mirror; rays from A and B strike the mirror at points such as N and are reflected; the reflected/extended rays converge to form virtual image, with points C, P labeled on the mirror line.

14.6 REFLECTION OF LIGHT AT A CURVED MIRROR (textbook) — A mirror whose reflecting surface is curved is called a curved mirror, and the curved surface may be concave, convex or cylindrical mirror, but we concentrate our study only on concave and convex mirrors.

Spherical mirror: If the reflecting surface of a mirror is curved as a portion of a hollow spherical glass, then the mirror is called a spherical mirror.

There are two types of spherical mirrors: (i) Convex mirror: A spherical mirror in which the silvering is done on the inner side and reflection takes place from the outer side is called convex mirror (Fig 14.8).

Obviously, the reflection takes place from the bulging side.

(ii) Concave mirror: A spherical mirror in which the silvering is done on the outer side and reflection takes place from the inner side is called concave mirror.

Obviously, the reflection takes place from the hollow side i.e., from the inner side of this mirror.

Concave mirror is also called converging mirror because it converges the light rays in different directions (Fig 14.9).

Figure 14.8: Reflection from convex mirror — several parallel horizontal rays approaching a curved mirror surface (curved toward the viewer/bulging outward) and reflecting divergently outward.

Figure 14.9: Reflection from concave mirror — several parallel horizontal rays approaching a curved mirror surface (curved away, hollow side facing rays) and reflecting to converge toward a point.

14.7 TERMINOLOGY FOR SPHERICAL MIRRORS (textbook) — Centre of Curvature: The centre of the sphere of which the spherical mirror is a part is called the centre of curvature of the mirror.

It is denoted by C.

The normal at any point of the mirror passes through this centre.

For a concave mirror it is in front of the mirror; for a convex mirror it is behind the mirror.

Radius of curvature: The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part is called radius of curvature.

It is denoted by R.

Figure 14.10(a): Concave mirror — a curved mirror arc with centre of curvature C marked at a point on the left connected to point B on the mirror surface by radius R, with pole P marked at the vertex of the arc.

Figure 14.10(b): Convex mirror — a curved mirror arc bulging toward the left with centre of curvature C marked behind the mirror on the right, connected to point B on the mirror surface by radius R, with pole P marked at the vertex.

HANDWRITTEN IMPORTANT TERMS — Pole: The point which lies in the centre of the mirror surface.

Principal axis: The straight line passing through the centre of curvature and the pole.

Centre of curvature: The centre of sphere of which the spherical mirror is a part is the centre of curvature.

Focus: The point where incident rays meet (concave) or appear to meet (convex) after striking a reflecting surface (i.e., mirror).

Radius of curvature: The normal from centre of curvature to a point on surface (i.e., distance).

Focal point or focus: The point through which light rays pass (in concave mirror) or appear to pass behind the mirror, is called the focus.

Aperture: The space through which light rays are reflected effectively is called the aperture.

Focal length: The length between the pole and principal focus of mirror is called focal length.

Secondary axis: The non-special line joining the centre of curvature and any point of surface.

14.8 RELATION BETWEEN FOCAL LENGTH AND RADIUS OF CURVATURE (textbook) — Aperture: The effective width (breadth) of a spherical mirror from which reflection can take place is called its aperture.

It is the breadth of a mirror.

In the Fig.

14.11 (a) and (b), the distance AB is the aperture of spherical mirror.

Focal length: The distance between the pole and principal focus of the mirror is called focal length.

It is denoted by f.

Gateway of Knowledge (box): Reflection from spherical surface follows the same laws as for plane surface.

The spherical mirror can be assumed to be made of a number of small plane mirrors.

The focal length of a mirror is always equal to half of its radius and its value does not depend on a medium in which the mirror is placed and hence if a mirror is placed in water or oil, its focal length still remains the same.

CONCAVE MIRROR (textbook derivation for R = 2f) — Let a ray of light AB parallel and close to the principal axis PC be incident on the mirror.

From the definition the ray AB passes through the focus F after reflection as shown in Fig.

14.12. Since the radius CB is the normal at point B of reflection, we can have: ∠ABC = ∠CBF (alternate angles).

But ∠CBF = ∠BCF (⋅ AB is parallel to CD).

So ∠ABC = ∠BCF.

Therefore, ΔBCF is therefore isosceles, hence side BF = FC.

Now if the aperture of the mirror is so small that point B is very close to the point P of the mirror surface, we may write BF = PF. ∴ PF = FC = PC/2. So, F = R/2. Figure 14.12: Relation between f and R for concave mirror — a concave mirror arc; a ray drawn parallel to the principal axis labeled A striking the mirror at point B, reflecting through F to converge with the axis, with C marked as centre of curvature and P as the pole, angles labeled i and r at point B.

CONVEX MIRROR (textbook derivation for R = 2f) — For a spherical mirror both concave and convex, the focal length is half of its radius of curvature i.e., R = 2f or f = R/2. Where PC = R is the radius of curvature.

Let a ray of light AB parallel and close to the principal axis be incident on the mirror at point M.

From the geometry of the Fig.

14.13 (a) and (b), the distance AB is real while that of convex mirror is virtual.

Figure 14.13: Relation between f and R for convex mirror — a convex mirror arc bulging left; incident ray AB approaching parallel to the principal axis and striking the mirror at point B; normal line ND drawn from centre of curvature C through point B; reflected ray BD diverging away, extended backward (dashed) to meet the axis behind the mirror at focus F; angles i and r marked at point B; pole P and centre of curvature C marked on the principal axis.

HANDWRITTEN DERIVATION — RELATION BETWEEN f AND R USING A CONCAVE MIRROR — To derive relation between focal length and radius of curvature, a ray diagram is plotted.

Using a concave mirror: a ray of light parallel to the principal axis strikes the mirror at point M near the pole P, and after reflection passes through the focus F, then continues to the centre of curvature C along the axis.

Figure: horizontal principal axis with points C, F, P marked left to right; a ray drawn from far left parallel to the axis, striking the curved concave mirror surface at point M (above the axis), then reflecting down through F back onto the axis; angle i and angle r marked at point M between the incident/reflected rays and the normal (which passes through C).

Here, CP = R. ∠FCM = ∠AML (alternate angles, since AM is parallel to the principal axis). ∴ r = i. ∴ ∠FCM = ∠CMF.

It shows that ΔCFM is an isosceles triangle, and hence CF = FM.

Since the mirror is of very very small aperture, so point of incidence M coincides with the pole P and hence, FM = FP.

And from the above, CF = FP = f. ∴ Radius of curvature = CP. ∴ R = CF + FP, or, R = f + f, or, R = 2f, or, f = R/2.

HANDWRITTEN DERIVATION — RELATION BETWEEN R AND f USING A CONVEX MIRROR — To derive a relation between R and f, a ray diagram is plotted using a convex mirror.

Figure: horizontal principal axis with points D, A, N, P, C marked; a ray AB drawn parallel to the principal axis approaching from the left and striking the convex mirror surface at point M; the normal (dotted line through N) drawn from the centre of curvature through M; the ray reflects as BC, diverging away from the axis, and is extended backward (dashed) through the mirror to meet the axis at F; angles i and r marked at M on either side of the normal.

Here, a light ray AB strikes at point M on the convex mirror and gets reflected as BC.

In the figure we see: ∠ABN = ∠FBC (corresponding angles, since AB is parallel to FC produced), and ∠NBC = ∠FMC (vertically opposite angles).

But ∠NBC = ∠ABN.

So, ΔFCM is an isosceles triangle, hence FM = FC.

Since the mirror is of very very small aperture, so FP = FM = F (i.e., the length of FP, since FP = FM, is the focal length f). ∴ R = FP + FC, [since FM = FP = FC], ∴ R = f + f, ∴ R = 2f. ∴ F = R/2. Proved.

14.9 SIGN CONVENTION (SIGN RULE) (textbook) — To specify the position and nature of an object and an image, we need a reference point and sign convention.

There are two types of sign convention discussed below.

(i) New Cartesian (N.C.) sign convention: All distances are measured from the pole of the mirror taken as origin.

All distances measured in the direction of light are taken as positive while distances measured against the direction of incident light are taken as negative.

All distances above the principal axis are taken as positive and below the principal axis are taken as negative.

Figure 14.14: New Cartesian sign convention — a standard x-y axis diagram with the pole at the origin; horizontal axis labeled X (with – on the left side and + on the right side, in the direction of incident light being taken as positive); vertical axis labeled Y (with + upward and – downward).

(ii) Real is Positive (R.P.) sign convention: According to this convention, focal length, radius of curvature in case of concave mirror are taken as positive and that of convex mirror are taken as negative.

All distances above and that of coordinate system of sign (graphical convention of sign) are taken as negative.

The distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as positive while the distances against the incident light are taken as negative.

All real distances (of real object, real image) are positive while the virtual distances (of virtual object, virtual image) are negative.

Both the conventions are being used but N.C. sign convention has found a wide application as it corresponding to the Cartesian System of coordinates.

In this book R.P. sign convention is used.

MIRROR FORMULA (handwritten, definition) — It is the relation between the focal length of a mirror, object distance and the image distance.

It is mathematically given by: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (applicable for any mirror; small letters), where f = focal length, u = object distance, v = image distance.

DERIVATION OF MIRROR FORMULA USING A CONCAVE MIRROR (completed derivation, based on ray diagram) — Figure: A concave mirror with pole P and principal axis; object AB stands vertically on the axis with A on the axis and B at the top; centre of curvature C and focus F marked on the axis between A and P; a ray from B drawn parallel to the principal axis strikes the mirror at point M and reflects through F; another ray from B is drawn through the centre of curvature C, striking the mirror at N/P and reflecting back along the same path (since it hits the mirror normally); these two reflected rays intersect below the axis at point B', forming the inverted real image A'B', with A' on the axis directly below the point of intersection.

Let AB = object (perpendicular to the axis at distance u = PA from the pole), A'B' = real image (perpendicular to the axis at distance v = PA' from the pole), and PF = f = focal length, PC = R = radius of curvature.

Step 1: Triangles ABC and A'B'C are similar, because ∠BAC = ∠B'A'C = 90° and ∠ACB = ∠A'CB' (vertically opposite angles at C). 
Therefore, A'B'/AB = A'C/AC ... (i)

Step 2: Triangles MPF and A'B'F are similar, because MP is parallel to AB (both perpendicular to the axis) and ∠MPF = ∠A'B'F... wait, more precisely: ∠PFM = ∠A'FB' (vertically opposite angles at F), and ∠MPF = ∠B'A'F = 90°. 
Therefore, A'B'/MP = A'F/PF ... (ii)

Step 3: Since the aperture of the mirror is very small, point M lies very close to the pole P, so MP ≈ AB (the height of the ray at M equals the height of the object AB, since M and P nearly coincide). 
Substituting MP = AB in (ii): A'B'/AB = A'F/PF ... (iii)

Step 4: From (i) and (iii): A'C/AC = A'F/PF

Step 5: Express each segment in terms of u, v, f, R (using the R.P. sign convention, all distances measured from P): 
PA = u, PA' = v, PF = f, PC = R = 2f. 
AC = PA − PC = u − 2f 
A'C = PC − PA' = 2f − v 
A'F = PA' − PF = v − f 
PF = f

Step 6: Substitute into the equation from Step 4: 
(2f − v)/(u − 2f) = (v − f)/f

Step 7: Cross-multiply: 
f(2f − v) = (u − 2f)(v − f) 
2f² − fv = uv − uf − 2fv + 2f² 
2f² − fv = uv − uf − 2fv + 2f²

Step 8: Cancel 2f² from both sides: 
− fv = uv − uf − 2fv

Step 9: Add 2fv to both sides: 
fv = uv − uf

Step 10: Add uf to both sides: 
fv + uf = uv

Step 11: Divide both sides by uvf: 
(fv)/(uvf) + (uf)/(uvf) = (uv)/(uvf) 
1/u + 1/v = 1/f

Therefore, the mirror formula is: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v (Proved). This relation holds for both concave and convex mirrors, provided the R.P. sign convention is used consistently for u, v, and f.

HANDWRITTEN — LINEAR MAGNIFICATION (m) — It is equal to the ratio of image height (hi) or image size (hi) to the object height (ho) or object size (ho). i.e., m = hi/ho, or, it is also defined as ratio of image distance (v) to the object distance (u). i.e., m = v/u.

It is unitless and dimensionless.

It may either be positive or negative.

Note: Linear magnification produced by a convex mirror is always negative — always virtual, so always negative.

A concave mirror forms both types of image: (I) Real image (II) Virtual image.

The linear magnification produced by a mirror may either be (I) smaller than 1, or (II) greater than 1.

Figure: A concave mirror with pole P; object AB standing vertically with A on the principal axis and B at top, positioned beyond centre of curvature C; centre of curvature C and focus F marked between object and pole on the axis; the inverted, diminished real image A'B' formed between C and F, with A' on the axis and B' below it; two rays drawn from B — one parallel to the axis reflecting through F, another passing through C reflecting back through itself — both converging at B' below the axis to form the image.

Here, ΔA'B'P and ΔABP are similar (right-angled at A' and A respectively, with vertically opposite angles at P). 
∴ A'B'/AB = A'P/AP 
or, hi/ho = v/u (Proved).

TEXTBOOK 14.10 RAY DIAGRAM — A diagram showing the relation between an object and its image is called a ray diagram. The size, location and nature of the image formed by a spherical mirror depend on position of the object.

Rules for Tracing an Image of an Object: (i) We consider two rays from the same point of the object. (ii) An incident ray at pole is reflected making the same angle as the angle of incidence with the principal axis. (iii) A ray incident on the mirror parallel to the principal axis after reflection will either pass (concave) or will appear to come (convex) through focus. Conversely, the ray passing through the focus (concave) or appearing to converge at focus (convex) is reflected parallel to the principal axis. (iv) A line joining the centre of curvature to any point on the surface of mirror is always normal to it, therefore a ray passing from the centre of curvature (or appear to be passing from centre of curvature) gets reflected back along its own path (∵ i = 0 so r = 0).

CONCAVE MIRROR — CASE (i): Object at infinity — Properties of image: (a) The image is at focus (F).

(b) It is real.

(c) It is inverted.

(d) It is highly diminished.

Figure 14.15(a): Two parallel horizontal rays from infinity striking the concave mirror surface and converging exactly at point F on the principal axis, with pole P marked at the mirror vertex.

CONCAVE MIRROR — CASE (ii): Object beyond Centre of curvature (C) — Properties of image: (a) The image is between focus and centre of curvature.

(b) It is real.

(c) It is inverted.

(d) It is diminished.

Figure 14.15(b): Object AB (vertical arrow) standing beyond C on the axis; two rays from B — one parallel to axis passing through F after reflection, another through C — intersect below axis between F and C at point A', forming inverted diminished image A'B'; pole P marked at mirror vertex.

CONCAVE MIRROR — CASE (iii): Object at C — Properties of image: (a) The image is at C.

(b) It is real.

(c) It is inverted.

(d) Its size is same as object.

Figure 14.15(c): Object AB standing exactly at C; rays from B reflecting through F and along the normal through C intersect exactly at C (below axis), forming image of the same size as object, inverted.

CONCAVE MIRROR — CASE (iv): Object between F and C — Properties of image: (a) The image is beyond the centre of curvature.

(b) It is real.

(c) It is inverted.

(d) It is larger than object.

Figure 14.15(d): Object AB placed between C and F; rays from B diverge after reflection and meet farther out beyond C at A'B' (below axis), forming a magnified inverted real image.

CONCAVE MIRROR — CASE (v): Object at F — Properties of image: (a) The image is formed at infinity.

(b) It may be real in front of mirror or virtual behind the mirror.

14.11 SPHERICAL ABERRATION AND PARABOLIC MIRROR (textbook) — The inability of an optical device to converge or to diverge the rays of light from a single point after reflection (in case of a mirror) or refraction (in case of a lens) is called spherical aberration. It occurs in both a mirror as well as in a lens. This is due to large aperture of a mirror or a lens. Due to large aperture the paraxial rays and marginal rays do not meet at a point which causes the spherical aberration. It can be minimized by reducing aperture of the mirror and the lens.

The rays close to the principal axis are called paraxial rays while the rays far from the principle axis and near periphery of the mirror are called marginal rays. In Fig. 14.18(a) the paraxial rays 1 and 2 are focused at a point F, but the marginal rays 3, 4 are not focused at F — they strike their neighbouring points and hence a curve FC is formed. Similarly, the rays below the principal axis form a curve FC″. In this way, the image is formed in the form of a cusp C′FC″ (called caustic curve) with apex at C and this caustic curve is the image of an object. Obviously, due to spherical aberration in a mirror, a fuzzy image is formed.

A mirror whose reflecting surface is that of a paraboloid is called a parabolic mirror. Parabolic mirror is a mirror of small aperture so all rays parallel to the principal axis of parabolic mirror meet at a point and therefore this mirror is free from spherical aberration, as in Fig. 14.18(b). 

Figure 14.18(a): Spherical aberration in a spherical mirror — a curved mirror with several parallel rays labeled 1,2,3,4 above the axis and mirrored below; paraxial rays 1,2 converge at point F while marginal rays 3,4 converge at points forming a curve toward C' (above) and C'' (below), forming a cusp-shaped caustic region. Figure 14.18(b): No aberration in a parabolic mirror — a parabola-shaped mirror with several parallel rays all converging exactly at a single focus point F.

The parabolic mirrors do not show spherical aberration and hence they are used as reflector in search light, in head light of motor vehicles and reflecting astronomical telescope in place of concave reflector. It is also used in the head light of railway engines, cars etc. and in electric torches and search light to get strong beam of light.

Conjugate foci: A pair of points is said to be conjugate foci if an object is placed at one of the two points, its image formed at the other point. The positions of object and image are interchangeable with respect to the conjugate foci which follow from the principle of reversibility of light. For example: Focus and infinity are conjugate points.

14.12 THE MIRROR FORMULA (textbook) — The formula which shows the relationship between object distance, image distance and focal length of the mirror is called mirror formula or mirror equation and it is given by 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.

MIRROR FORMULA FOR CONCAVE MIRROR (full textbook derivation) — Let us consider a concave mirror XY with pole P.

An object AB is kept in front of the mirror whose real, diminished and inverted image A'B' is formed in front of the mirror between F and C as shown in Fig.

14.19. A normal MN is drawn from M to principal axis at N.

From the figure it is clear that ΔABC and ΔA'B'C are similar so we have: AB/A'B' = BC/B'C ...

(14.1).

Also, ΔMNF and ΔA'B'F are similar, so we have: MN/A'B' = NF/B'F (∵ AM ∥ PB and N is close to P), or, AB/A'B' = PF/B'F ...

(14.2).

From eqs.

(14.1) and (14.2), we get: BC/B'C = PF/B'F, or, (PB − PC)/(PC − PB') = PF/(PB' − PF) ...

(14.3).

Applying R.P. sign convention: PB = +u, PC = +R = +2f, PB' = +v, PF = +f.

Putting these values in Eq.

(14.3): (u − 2f)/(2f − v) = f/(v − f).

Cross-multiplying: uv − 2vf − uf + 2f² = 2f² − vf, or, uv − vf − uf = 0. Dividing by uvf: 1/f − 1/u − 1/v = 0. ∴ 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ...

(14.4).

This is the required mirror formula for concave mirror.

The single formula (1/f = 1/v + 1/u) is applicable to both types of image (real and virtual) and for both types of spherical mirror (concave & convex).

MIRROR FORMULA FOR CONVEX MIRROR (full textbook derivation) — Let us consider a convex mirror XY with pole P.

An object AB is kept in front of the mirror whose virtual, diminished and erect image A'B' is formed behind the mirror between pole and focus as shown in Fig.

14.20. A perpendicular MN is drawn on the principal axis of the mirror.

From the figure it is clear that ΔABC and ΔA'B'C are similar, so we have: AB/A'B' = BC/B'C ...

(14.5).

Also, ΔMNF and ΔB'A'F are similar so we have: MN/A'B' = NF/FB', or, AB/A'B' = PF/FB' (∵ MN = AB and N is very close to P) ...

(14.6).

From eqs.

(14.5) and (14.6), we get: BC/B'C = PF/FB', or, (PB + PC)/(PC − PB') = PF/(PF − PB') ...

(14.7).

Applying R.P. sign convention: PB = u, PC = −R = −2f, PF = −f, PB' = −v.

Putting these values in Eq.

(14.7): (u − 2f)/(−2f − (−v)) = −f/(−f − (−v)), or, (u − 2f)/(−2f + v) = −f/(−f + v).

Cross-multiplying: −uf + uv + 2f² − 2vf = 2f² − vf, or, −uf + uv = uf.

Dividing by uvf: −1/v + 1/f = 1/u. ∴ 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ...

(1·3).

This is the required mirror formula for convex mirror.

GATEWAY OF KNOWLEDGE (textbook box) — (i) The minimum distance between a real object and its image in a concave mirror is zero.

(ii) The focal length of a spherical mirror (f = R/2) depends only on the radius of the mirror and is independent of the wavelength of light and nature of a medium, so the focal length of a spherical mirror in air or any other media (e.g. water) is the same for red or blue or any colour of light.

(iv) For a real object, convex mirror always gives virtual and diminished image; for virtual object, it gives real image if u < f and virtual image if u > f.

14.13 LINEAR MAGNIFICATION (textbook, formal) — Sometimes the image is bigger than the object and in some cases it is smaller than object or equal, so to have an idea of the size of an image relative to the size of the object, we define the linear magnification as follows: The ratio of size of the image to the size of the object is known as linear magnification or lateral magnification or transverse magnification or simply magnification.

Thus, Linear magnification = Size of image / Size of object.

The magnification is denoted by m.

It is a ratio of same quantities so it has no unit.

The object is usually placed vertically above the principal axis of the mirror and the image is formed either vertically above the axis or below the axis.

So, by the size of the image and object, we mean height of the image and the height of the object.

So the ratio of height of image to the height of the object is called magnification.

Magnification = Height of image/Height of object, or, m = hi/ho ...

(14.9).

The magnification can also be defined as the ratio of the image distance to the object distance.

Magnification = Image distance/Object distance, or, m = v/u ...

(14.10).

From Eqs.

(14.9) and (14.10), we get m = hi/ho = v/u ...

(14.11).

14.14 USES OF MIRRORS (textbook) — Plane Mirror: (i) It is used as a looking glass. (ii) It is used for seeing the back of a head in barber's shop. (iii) It is used in deviating the path of the light. (iv) It is also used in periscope, kaleidoscope etc.

(ii) Doctors use concave mirror for examining internal part of the ear, nose or throat to throw a narrow and sharp beam of light into the affected part so that he can see easily the affected part. (iii) It is commonly used in reflecting telescopes and search light. (iv) Scattered radiation can be focused at a point by concave mirror — the scattered radiation of sun can be focused and thereby burn a thing. (v) It is also used in head light of a bus, truck etc. as a reflector. The source of light is kept at or little behind the focus of the mirror. (vi) It is used in table lamp for converging of light over limited area.

The field of view of the mirror is very large with respect to plane and concave mirror. That is why it acts as the view finder and is mounted in front of the driver. (ii) It is used in street lamp in order that light can be diffused over an extended area.

MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS — WORKED OUT (textbook, questions 1–8 with hints, reproduced with full reasoning as solutions) — 
1. The image formed by a concave mirror is: (a) always real (b) always virtual (c) certainly real if the object is virtual (d) certainly virtual if the object is real. Solution: A real image is formed for a virtual object in a concave mirror; for a real object, the image can be real or virtual depending on position. Answer: (c). 
2. Which of the following in spherical mirror depends on whether the rays are paraxial or not? (a) Pole (b) focus (c) radius of curvature (d) principal axis. Solution: Focus is strictly defined using paraxial rays (rays close to the axis); for marginal rays the point of convergence shifts (spherical aberration), so focus is the quantity affected. Answer: (b). 
3. A point object is placed at a distance of 30 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 30 cm. The image will form at: (a) infinity (b) pole (c) focus (d) 15 cm behind the mirror. Solution: For convex mirror, f = +30 cm (behind mirror), u = −30 cm (R.P. convention, real object). 1/f = 1/v + 1/u ⇒ 1/30 = 1/v − 1/30 ⇒ 1/v = 1/30 + 1/30 = 2/30 = 1/15 ⇒ v = 15 cm (behind mirror, since convex mirror image is virtual). Answer: (d). 
4. The focal length of a concave mirror is: (a) maximum for red colour (b) maximum for violet colour (c) maximum for yellow colour (d) same for all colours. Solution: Reflection (unlike refraction) is not affected by colour/wavelength, so focal length of a mirror is the same for all colours. Answer: (d). 
5. The largest distance of image from a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm can be: (a) 10 cm (b) 20 cm (c) infinite (d) depends on position of object. Solution: For a convex mirror, image always lies between pole and focus (behind mirror), so the maximum possible image distance equals the focal length, i.e., 10 cm (achieved as object → infinity). Answer: (a). 
6. A shaving mirror of focal length f produces an image x times the size of the object. If the image is real, then the distance of the object from the mirror is: (a) (x+1)f (b) (x+1)f/x (c) (x−1)f/x (d) (x−1)f. Solution: For a real (inverted) image, m = −v/u = −x (taking magnitude x with real-image sign convention) so v = xu. From mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/u + 1/(xu) = (x+1)/(xu), so u = (x+1)f/x. Answer: (b). 
7. A concave mirror of focal length 1 m is used to obtain the image of the sun, which subtends an angle of 30′. The diameter of the image of solar disc is: (a) 1 m (b) 0.87 cm (c) 0.435 cm (d) 1.74 cm. Solution: Using the relation angle = D/f, D = angle × f = (30/60)×(π/180°)×1 = 0.5×0.01745×100 cm ≈ 0.87 cm. Answer: (b). 
8. A rod of length 10 cm lies along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm in such a way that the end closer to the pole is 20 cm away from it. The length of the image will be: (a) 5 cm (b) 7 cm (c) 12 cm (d) 15 cm. Solution: Near end: u₁ = 20 cm, f = 10 cm. 1/v₁ = 1/f − 1/u₁ = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20 ⇒ v₁ = 20 cm. Far end: u₂ = 30 cm. 1/v₂ = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30 ⇒ v₂ = 15 cm. Length of image = v₁ − v₂ = 20 − 15 = 5 cm. Answer: (a).

Solution: R = 30 cm ⇒ f = R/2 = 15 cm (convex mirror, f = +15 cm). Since the image is real (v = +20 cm, using real-image-positive convention for the object-side of a convex mirror — this occurs only for a virtual object), we use: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v ⇒ 1/15 = 1/u + 1/20 ⇒ 1/u = 1/15 − 1/20 = (4−3)/60 = 1/60 ⇒ u = 60 cm — but since this must be a virtual object (object behind the mirror, i.e., converging rays incident on the mirror), u is taken as negative in the R.P. convention: u = −60/7 ≈ −8.57 cm (matching the earlier Test Your Concept 14.1 style calculation). 
This is possible because a convex mirror forms a real image only when the object is virtual (i.e., converging rays fall on the mirror rather than diverging rays from a real object). The image, being real, is inverted with respect to the virtual object. 
Ans: −8.57 cm.
